wages_japan_real_index.name: Real wages · Japan (1932=100)
wages_japan_real_index.definition: Published real-wage index for selected male industrial wage series, deflated using the source cost-of-living index. 100 is the 1932 reference; 50 indicates half that reference purchasing power within this series. It is not a basket count, money amount, or cross-country living-standard level. The nominal and cost-of-living series are linked/rebased by the author; no additional Atlas inflation adjustment or interpolation.
wages_japan_real_index.caveat: Japanese industrial wage statistics selected and linked by the author; not all workers or household incomes. Survey coverage changes: 1909 factories with 10+ workers, Bank of Japan series with 30+, later monthly survey about 50+. No historical-border or imperial-territory match is assumed.

The reported carpenter wages between 1897-1921 stated that these workers also received “board and lodging”.

AAOWD_TGO.citation: Frankema & van Waijenburg (2023), What about the race between education and technology in the Global South? Comparing skill premiums in colonial Africa and Asia. Economic History Review 76:941–978, doi:10.1111/ehr.13221. AAOWD v1.0 (July 2020).

workbookNotes: Sources
These data were supplied by Ewout Frankema (Wageningen University) and Marlous van Waijenburg (University of Michigan 2017-2020/Harvard Business School starting July 2020) citing the sources below:
The construction and application of the data are explained in:
Ewout Frankema and Marlous van Waijenburg (2019), "The Great Convergence: Skill Accumulation and Mass Education in Africa and Asia, 1870-2010" CEPR Discussion Paper 14150
cepr.org/active/publications/discussion_papers/dp.php?dpno=14150
Underlying primary sources
BG
The Budgets Generals that contain detailed lists on the (former) French territories
OI
The ILO’s annually conducted ‘October Inquiry’
These surveys contain wage information on various occupations and were conducted between 1950-2008. These surveys were published in the following publications:
1950-1957: Yearbook of Labour Statistics
1950-1963: International Labour Review Statistical Supplement
1964-2008: Bulletin of Labour Statistics October Inquiry Results
Notes
No LaborSta file was extracted for Togo
Note that the years 1982-1983 (mechanics) were omitted due to a strange trend break in the nominal wage series that was not observed for the other artisans - omissions indicated in red
Funding
European Research Council Grant Agreement no. 313114
Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research VIDI Grant no. 016.124.307
University of Michigan MITRE Grant no. 333797

BB
The colonial Blue Books that contain statistics on the (former) British territories
OI
The ILO’s annually conducted ‘October Inquiry’
These surveys contain wage information on various occupations and were conducted between 1950-2008. These surveys were published in the following publications:
1950-1957: Yearbook of Labour Statistics
1950-1963: International Labour Review Statistical Supplement
1964-2008: Bulletin of Labour Statistics October Inquiry Results
SP
The Sessional Papers contain various departmental reports for the former British colonies
Notes
Note that we redid our original JEH series for the year before 1919, as the unskilled rate for those years was extrapolated backwards on the basis of a fixed carpenter-laborer SP.

Note that we dropped the year 1954 from the OI as these were minimum wages only and did not capture the scope of skilled labor (it created a significant deviation in skill-premiums from the rates reported in the SPs) - omissions indicated in red
LaborSta sheet UGA_O1_1983-2008 extracted on 18/08/2012
Note that we did not include a series for clerks and bank tellers out of concerns about the inclusion of Asian labor - omissions indicated in red

AAOWD_ZMB.title: Frankema & van Waijenburg · Zambia occupational wages
AAOWD_ZMB.language: English compilation; underlying French, English, Dutch and other colonial records
AAOWD_ZMB.citation: Frankema & van Waijenburg (2023), What about the race between education and technology in the Global South? Comparing skill premiums in colonial Africa and Asia. Economic History Review 76:941–978, doi:10.1111/ehr.13221. AAOWD v1.0 (July 2020).

workbookNotes: Sources
These data were supplied by Ewout Frankema (Wageningen University) and Marlous van Waijenburg (University of Michigan 2017-2020/Harvard Business School starting July 2020) citing the sources below:
The construction and application of the data are explained in:
Ewout Frankema and Marlous van Waijenburg (2019), "The Great Convergence: Skill Accumulation and Mass Education in Africa and Asia, 1870-2010" CEPR Discussion Paper 14150
cepr.org/active/publications/discussion_papers/dp.php?dpno=14150
Note that for category-years where we had data available from both colonial sources and ILO sources, we used both series
In such cases, the final skill-premium used in the accompanying paper is the average of the two resulting skill-premium series
Underlying primary sources
BB
The colonial Blue Books that contain statistics on the (former) British territories
OI
The ILO’s annually conducted ‘October Inquiry’
These surveys contain wage information on various occupations and were conducted between 1950-2008. These surveys were published in the following publications:
1950-1957: Yearbook of Labour Statistics
1950-1963: International Labour Review Statistical Supplement
1964-2008: Bulletin of Labour Statistics October Inquiry Results
SP
The Sessional Papers contain various departmental reports for the former British colonies
Notes
Note that the year 1953 (carpenters) was omitted due to a strange trend break in the nominal wage series from both the SPs and the ILO - omission indicated in red
Note that we used the average of minimum and maximum rates (carpenters) for the 1950s instead of a lognormal based on wage distribution tables

Note that the years 1961-1964 (carpenters, electricians, and mechanics) were omitted due to concerns about a race premium (nominal wage series suddenly increase more than 10-fold and do not have explicit annotation that these refer to African wages) - omissions indicated in red
No LaborSta file was extracted for Zambia
Note that years before 1975 (bank tellers) were excluded, as these referred to Europeans - omissions indicated in red
Note that the years 1976 (mechanics), steno-dactylographer 1977-8, and 1991 (bank tellers) were omitted as they generated a negative value - omissions indicated in red
Funding
European Research Council Grant Agreement no. 313114
Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research VIDI Grant no. 016.124.307
University of Michigan MITRE Grant no. 333797
